                                            PROJECT NO. 58481


     RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                              §                BEFORE THE
    LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                            §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                         §                 OF TEXAS


      ERCOT STEEL MILLS’ COMMENTS ON STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT OF
                      PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.194

        The ERCOT Steel Mills 1 offer the following comments on the discussion draft issued by
the Staff of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission), which would propose new 16
Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards.


                                              INTRODUCTION

        The ERCOT Steel Mills appreciate the efforts to implement Senate Bill 6 (SB6)2 and
specifically §37.0561 of the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) by establishing clear and
transparent standards for interconnecting large load customers in ERCOT’s power region. Well-
designed interconnection standards are essential for managing the risk of stranded infrastructure
costs and for maintaining system reliability. At the same time, these standards must also support
continued investment and business growth for both existing and prospective customers
interconnecting to the ERCOT grid. To achieve this balance, it is important that new
interconnection requirements are reasonable and consistent, administrative processes are efficient
for new loads, utilities, ERCOT, and the Commission, and final implementation is consistent with
the intent of SB6.

        PURA §37.0561 was enacted to address concerns associated with interconnecting
significant new loads to the ERCOT grid, particularly high-demand loads that could “significantly
impact transmission needs.”3 The ERCOT Steel Mills offer the comments below to highlight how


1
  The ERCOT Steel Mills include CMC Steel Texas, Gerdau Long Steel North America, Nucor Steel-Texas, a division
of Nucor Corporation, and Steel Dynamics, Inc.
2
       Senate       Bill      6       (89th     R.S.,     2025)     (Sen.       Phil      King),    available      at
https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/pdf/SB00006F.pdf#navpanes=0.
3
  PURA §37.0561(c) ("The standards must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded interconnection
where the total load at a single site would exceed a demand threshold established by the commission based on the size
of loads that significantly impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power region").


                                                                                                                   1
 potential implementation of the draft rule could affect investment decisions, financial exposure,
and operational certainty for existing customers, even where proposed load additions are modest.
As currently written, the proposed definition of a “large load customer” in draft §25.194(b) could
be misinterpreted and potentially implemented in a manner that is inconsistent with the intent of
SB6. The draft rule should be clarified and implemented to avoid unintended consequences for
existing industrial facilities seeking to make investments and process upgrades that do not
materially impact the transmission grid and do not carry significant risk of stranded costs if the
load does not materialize.


                              COMMENTS ON DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194

A.       Proposed 16 TAC §25.194(b), Definitions

         1.       Interpretation Risks Related to the Definition of a Large Load Customer in
                  Proposed §25.194(b)(7)

         As drafted, a large load customer is defined as “[a] customer requesting a new or expanded
interconnection where the customer’s total peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75
megawatts.”4 SB6 requires that “[the interconnection] standards must apply only to customers
requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a
demand threshold established by the commission based on the size of loads that significantly
impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power region.” SB6 additionally sets the demand
threshold at a presumptive level of 75 MW. 5

         The ERCOT Steel Mills are concerned that this definition may, without clarification, be
misinterpreted to apply to all expanded interconnections for load additions, no matter how modest,
at an existing industrial facility that already exceeds 75 MWs of peak demand.

         This definition could be misinterpreted and implemented to inappropriately extend the
application of large load interconnection standards to scenarios beyond the focus of SB6 on


4
  Proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code §25.194(b)(7).
5
  PURA §37.0561(c) sets the demand threshold at “75 megawatts unless the commission determines that a lower
threshold is necessary to accomplish the purposes described by Subsection (b).” Those purposes are to “support
business development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining
system reliability.” PURA §37.0561(b).


                                                                                                                      2
 managing substantial new loads entering the system. By way of example, an existing nominal 100
MW industrial load that seeks to add a 10 MW minor process line or replace and/or upgrade
existing equipment should not be subject to expansive new interconnection requirements that are
intended only for load additions that materially impact the transmission grid and carry significant
risk of stranded costs if the load does not materialize.

       Such an interpretation would also unjustly treat new and existing facilities differently, since
a new load would have to meet the 75 MW threshold to become a large load customer, whereas an
expansion of an existing facility, which is already in excess of 75 MWs, would not have to meet
any additional threshold to be considered a large load customer. (As an example, under this
interpretation, adding 5 MW to a new site would not be considered a large load customer, but
adding 5 MW to a site already exceeding 75 MW would be a large load customer.)

       From an economic development and investment perspective, this interpretation could have
unintended consequences for existing industrial facilities seeking to make routine improvements
or minor expansions. For steel mills, incremental load additions are often tied to modernization
projects or operational enhancements, including furnace or rolling-mill equipment replacement
upgrades, higher-efficiency motors and drives, and improved process controls. If such projects are
perceived to trigger new compliance obligations based on total site demand, rather than the
magnitude of the additional load, customers may forego investments, invest less efficiently at a
new location with total site load under the threshold, or decide to invest out of state to avoid
excessive regulatory costs on minor load additions or increasing complexity on managing the
current site load. Overall, this dynamic could discourage facilities from pursuing necessary
investments to remain competitive, even when those projects do not meaningfully affect
transmission planning, reliability, or stranded-cost risk.

       In order to clarify the definition of a large load customer to address these concerns, the
ERCOT Steel Mills recommend the following edit to proposed §25.194(b)(7):

       (7)     Large load customer -- A customer requesting a new or expanded
               interconnection where the customer's total additional peak demand at a
               single site is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW).




                                                                                                    3
         2.       Clarifying Edits to Additional Definitions Consistent with Changes to the
                 Definition of Large Load Customer (§25.194(b)(2) and (11))

        In addition to the revision to the definition of large load customer discussed above,
additional minor edits would be helpful to clarify the definitions of “Contracted peak demand” and
“Requested peak demand” such that the associated obligations in the proposed rule only apply to
additional load of 75 MW or more. ERCOT Steel Mills are concerned that these definitions, as
proposed, may lead to overbroad imposition of requirements on existing load.

        For example, under the current draft rule, financial security requirements related to the
discretionary services agreement in proposed §25.194(e)(8) and the intermediate agreement in
proposed §25.194(h)(8) are tied to a customer’s requested or contracted peak demand, which
reflects the total amount of load requested to be served at a site under an executed agreement. 6 For
existing industrial facilities, contracted peak demand could represent cumulative load that has
already been interconnected and supported by the grid for many years. If the large load customer
definition is interpreted to apply broadly based on total site demand, incremental expansions could
result in substantial financial commitments being associated with legacy load that does not drive
new transmission risk.

        In order to clarify that these financial security requirements only apply to additional
demand (whether at a new or existing facility), the ERCOT Steel Mills offer the following
limited edits to the definition of contracted peak demand in §25.194(b)(2) and requested peak
demand in §25.194(b)(11):

        (2)      Contracted peak demand - the total additional peak demand that a large
                 load customer requests that an interconnecting electric utility serve at a site
                 as stated in an executed and securitized discretionary services agreement or
                 intermediate agreement.

        (11)    Requested peak demand -- the total additional peak demand that a large
                load customer requests, prior to executing and securitizing a discretionary
                services agreement, intermediate agreement, or interconnection agreement,
                that an interconnecting electric utility serve.



6
 Proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code §25.194(e)(8) ("Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. A large load customer
must pay financial security to the interconnecting electric utility $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand


                                                                                                              4
 B.        Proposed 16 TAC §25.194(l), ERCOT Operational Standards

          The draft rule provides that ERCOT may establish “operational standards” developed by
ERCOT for large load customers as a condition of interconnection and continued operation. This
proposed language is overbroad and grants ERCOT authority to impose potentially significant
barriers to operation for large load customers. SB6 does not authorize ERCOT to impose
operational standards except to require large load customers with on-site backup generating
facilities that can serve at least 50 percent of on-site demand to be able to either deploy those on-
site backup generating facilities or curtail load. 7 Going beyond this requirement would create
significant risks for existing and interconnecting load. The ERCOT Steel Mills, therefore,
recommend the Commission delete this proposed section in its entirety.

          In addition to the concerns raised above, when read in conjunction with the site-level large
load customer definition as is currently proposed, this provision could possibly be interpreted to
apply new operational standards to an existing facility over 75 MW already operating in Texas that
may be adding modest incremental load. For existing industrial facilities, this creates uncertainty
regarding whether new operational obligations could apply to load already in operation for many
years. Without a clearer, limited definition of operational standards and how they would apply,
businesses may have difficulty assessing the scope and potential impact of such standards when
planning whether to invest in their operations. If subsection (l) is not deleted as recommended,
then at a minimum, these standards should be clearly limited to new, additional loads equal to or
in excess of 75 MW.

C.        New Proposed 16 TAC §25.194(l), Good cause exception

          Given the risk of unintended consequences from implementing these new interconnection
standards, it may be useful for the Commission to be able to address issues impacting individual
large load customers on a case-by-case basis. Therefore, the Commission should implement a
process whereby large load customers may, upon a showing of good cause, request that the
Commission waive or grant an exception to any of the requirements in this proposed rule.
16 TAC §25.3(b) already allows the Commission to make exceptions to any of its substantive rules



7
    PURA §37.0561(e).


                                                                                                    5
 for good cause,8 and the Commission specifically allows applicants to request good cause
exceptions in other proceedings.9 Similarly, such a process in the case of interconnecting large load
customers would also allow the Commission to remain nimble and respond to specific issues raised
by large load customers. Therefore, the ERCOT Steel Mills recommend the Commission adopt
a new proposed section allowing large load customers to request the Commission waive or
grant an exception to any of the requirements in this proposed rule.

        (l)      Good cause exception -- Upon a showing of good cause, a large load
                 customer may request that the commission waive or grant an exception to
                 any requirement of this section.

                                               CONCLUSION

        The ERCOT Steel Mills raise the following concerns and recommendations to highlight
the risk that the draft rule could be misinterpreted and applied beyond its intended scope, namely,
to situations other than the addition of significant new load exceeding 75 MW. The Commission
should consider whether providing additional clarity would help ensure that the rule is
implemented consistently with the Legislature’s focus in SB6. Such clarity is essential to avoid
unintended consequences for the Texas economy, particularly the inappropriate application of new
standards to existing industrial facilities undergoing investments or process upgrades that do not
materially impact the transmission grid or create a significant risk of stranded costs if the load does
not materialize.

        The ERCOT Steel Mills appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments and look
forward to continued collaboration with the Commission and stakeholders.

ERCOT STEEL MILLS’ COMMENTS ON STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT OF NEW 16
                          TAC §25.194

                                   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The ERCOT Steel Mills offer the following considerations regarding the Commission Staff’s
discussion draft of proposed 16 TAC §25.194:
•   Clarification of the Large Load Customer Definition: The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend
    that the definition of a “large load customer” should be revised and clarified to limit new
    interconnection standards to additional (i.e., new or increased) load (total additional peak
    demand) above the threshold.
       •   This clarification would implement the proposed interconnection standards consistent
           with the intent of Senate Bill 6 and reduce the risk of unintended policy outcomes for
           existing industrial facilities pursuing incremental load additions, where customers may
           otherwise delay or forgo routine investments and operational upgrades, even when such
           projects do not materially affect transmission planning, reliability, or stranded-cost risk.
•   Clarification of Additional Definitions Consistent with Large Load Customer Definition:
    The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend that the definitions of “Contract peak demand” and
    “Requested peak demand” be modified consistent with the recommended update to the
    definition of large load customers (total additional peak demand) to clarify that the standards
    apply only to additional (i.e., new or increased) load above the 75 MW threshold.
       •   For example, the rules should clarify that any applicable financial security requirements
           should be applied only to the additional contracted or requested peak demand.
           Including legacy load that is not part of the increased interconnection request would
           create an excessive financial burden for incremental load additions.
•   ERCOT Operational Standards: The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend deleting this proposed
    section in its entirety. This section, as proposed, would grant ERCOT overbroad powers to
    impose operational standards on large load customers.

•   Good Cause Exception: The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend adding a new proposed section
    allowing large load customers to request the Commission waive or grant an exception to any
    of the requirements in this proposed rule. Such a rule would allow the Commission to respond
    to unintended consequences that arise on a case-by-case basis.

It is critical that this draft rule is implemented consistently with the intent of Senate Bill 6 in a
manner that addresses significant new load while avoiding unintended consequences for existing
industrial facilities.
